absent: Handler behavior for remote callbacks and completion signaling is not shown in these fragments.
Descriptor lock and wait primitives, queue layout, and interrupt entry handling are not shown.
Numeric values of call-function flags, primitive selectors, and seccomp modes are not shown.
Torture thread creation, stop, must-stop, and stutter deadline production are not shown.
Statistics thread, free-list maintenance, selector table building, and module parameters beyond names are not shown.
Seccomp enforcement, filter lifecycle, reply path, and addfd completion handling are not shown.
Architecture specific IPI senders and trace event definitions are not shown.

findings.text: Broadcast invocation service requests a caller supplied routine with opaque context on processors selected by a caller mask, with a boolean selecting synchronous waiting. It forwards to a conditional core with no per-target predicate and maps the boolean to an internal wait flag.

All-online invocation service requests a routine with opaque context on every online processor, with integer wait control. It forwards to the same conditional core over the current online set with no predicate.

Remote work is considered only when the caller mask intersects the online set excluding the caller. The effective remote set is the intersection with online minus the local processor, further pruned by an optional predicate, with notified processors tracked separately for dispatch.

Notification cost follows the number of newly kicked processors: none when no queue transitions from empty occur, a single-target signal for one, and a mask signal for several. Concurrent mask changes may legitimately yield zero.

Local execution is independent of remote queuing and happens only when a run-local flag is present, the caller mask still contains the local processor, and the optional predicate accepts it. The routine runs with local interrupts held off and then restored.

Caller is expected to run in task context with interrupts enabled when online outside crash and early-boot exception windows; violations are warned. Preemption is held across mask selection, queuing and dispatch while per-processor or task-local scratch storage is in use, then released before any synchronous completion wait.

Synchronous use risks deadlock if interrupt delivery is blocked between queue insertion and IPI transmission, while asynchronous use risks deadlock through shared per-target descriptor storage between caller and interrupt handling. Operation with interrupts disabled is explicitly called out as deadlock prone.

Two build configurations exist for task-associated IPI scratch storage: one returns a per-task pointer or an inlined value depending on a static branch, the other always reports absence and forces fallback to caller-processor storage.
Mask IPI transmission first emits a trace event identifying the generic call-function interrupt path and caller address, then delegates to an architecture specific mask sender.

Each torture iteration exercises one randomly weighted primitive among reschedule, single, single-RPC, many and all families, maintaining separate attempt and overflow counters per mode and wait flavor.

An optional global CPU-read lock may surround queuing; the RPC variant temporarily drops it across completion waiting and reacquires it afterward. Descriptor allocation uses atomic context and failure is counted rather than blocking.

For waiting invocations the harness validates that remote completion became visible; on multiprocessor or single-target runs a missing completion indication triggers a one-time warning plus an error counter increment and intentional leaking of the descriptor to avoid reuse after possible concurrent completion.

Per-thread driver pins itself to an assigned processor with low priority, optionally delays for holdoff, barriers with peers on a shared start count, then loops invoking the single-operation driver while tolerating offline intervals by reapplying affinity, yielding and honoring global stutter, until a stop request.

Torture initialization refuses concurrent runs, normalizes negative and all-nonpositive weight tables into effective selection weights, registers optional hotplug, shutdown and stutter helpers, and starts a configured number of invoker threads plus an optional statistics thread, unwinding through common cleanup on failure.

Teardown marks completion, stops invokers, issues a synchronous broadcast with an empty handler to drain pending callbacks, stops statistics, prints results, releases statistics storage, drains per-processor free lists, and classifies outcome as failure, hotplug mismatch, or success.

Only one torture personality may be active; initialization under a global mutex rejects a second type, records type and verbosity, resets stop state and start time, and emits parameters, while the matching end releases the mutex and arms a reboot notifier.

Cleanup start serializes with init and shutdown through a global mutex, rejecting concurrent module removal during system shutdown with a delay and failure return, otherwise marking removal state before stopping helpers outside the mutex; cleanup finish clears the active type under the same mutex.

Shuffle teardown unregisters every registered shuffle participant under its dedicated mutex, freeing each list element, then stops the background shuffler and releases its temporary mask storage, leaving a null handle.
Shuffle participant list mutation is protected by a dedicated mutex held across traversal and deletion of all entries.

Each optional helper has idempotent stop logic that does nothing when never started and otherwise stops its thread and clears its handle, with shutdown handling also unregistering its reboot notifier. Startup helpers record their parameters and create their thread only when their interval or count is positive.
Hotplug health is defined as exact match between attempted and successful online and offline transitions when hotplug is configured; without hotplug support failure is never reported.

Stutter waiting inserts an RCU quiescent point then sleeps until a global absolute deadline when in the future and absorbs shutdown requests, reporting whether stalling occurred. The helper sleep optionally adds bounded fuzz to a base duration, marks the caller idle, and delegates to high-resolution timeout waiting.

Notification descriptor associates a target task, a unique per-filter cookie, borrowed filter data valid for the whole lifecycle, a three-state progression field, reply payload fields meaningful only after reply, a completion for state changes, and list links for global queuing plus outstanding descriptor-add requests.
A user notification starts in init, moves to sent after user retrieval, returns to init if interrupted by a signal requiring redelivery, and moves to replied upon handler response.

Descriptor-add request carries a file reference, numeric descriptor, control flags and ioctl flags, a completion and list link, plus a union that interprets the same storage as a boolean request option before reply and an integer status after reply.
Filter notification queue head holds an atomic outstanding-request count, control flags, a monotonically assigned next cookie, and a list of pending kernel notifications.
Decision cache holds a native-action bitmap sized by native architecture count and, when compat support is configured, a second bitmap sized by compat count.
Terminal seccomp mode value is defined as one past the filter mode value.
A notification identifier validity ioctl number is defined with read direction, index two, and 64-bit payload width, reserved for wrong-direction probing.
Per-processor shadow-call-stack cache depth is fixed at two entries.
All seccomp log output shares a common subsystem prefix applied by the module format macro.
Shadow-stack enablement is tracked by a default-false static key. Per-processor caches hold two pointers; processor offline cleanup releases each slot and clears it, always reporting success.
